articles.title_orig: Italy’s PM deploys troops as nation faces widespread strikes and port blockades
articles.title_zh: Italy’s PM deploys troops as nation faces widespread strikes and port blockades
articles.content_orig:
ROME — Tens of thousands of people took to the streets of Rome, Milan and other Italian cities Friday as part of nationwide demonstrations against the cost of living and high military spending.
The demonstrations were largely peaceful but an NBC News crew saw police use a water cannon on protesters and groups of police charging to disperse protesters in Rome on Friday night.
After several weeks of violent protests in Italy and throughout Europe , more widespread disruption is expected after the Unione Sindacale di Base (USB) and other trade unions called on workers in both the public and private sectors to strike and protest.
The demonstrations in Italy appear to have been partly inspired by those in France , where some of the worst rioting in decades erupted in cities across the country after student protests about the state of education in the country evolved into wider actions about the cost of living and social security.
Elsewhere in Europe, a huge encampment of tents has occupied a square in Madrid since late last month, and thousands of people in Portugal have taken to the streets in the city of Lisbon. Tear gas and water cannons were also used on black-clad protesters in Brussels.
In Rome, many waved communist and Palestinian flags, as well as signs against the Iran war. Some let off pink smoke bombs. There was a jovial mood among the demonstrators as they lined up before the march, as has often been the case early on at previous protests, only for violence to break out later.
Protesters storm the Colosseum in Rome
Giovanna Di Matteo, a member of the left-wing Potere al Popolo! party, said she was protesting against the government that “did nothing for the people of this country.”
The government had spent money on the military “while they cut on welfare, they cut on services and people cannot reach the end of the month,” she said. “They have no money for their houses, they have no money for gasoline and everything.”
Luca, a 20-year-old medical student said the protesters felt they were “still not being heard, that everything is still the same,” and the government didn’t “care about our voice, about our voices, and about the future of this nation that is our nation.”
“We have been completely screwed by the fact that the wages do not keep up on inflation and the wages in general do not keep up with the cost of living,” added Luca, who asked to have his last name withheld out of fear of repercussions from law enforcement.
Major demonstrations also took place in other cities and towns across Italy.
They came after a number of protests in recent weeks have turned violent. Groups of masked protesters looted stores in Milan and elsewhere and threw projectiles at police, who responded with tear gas and water cannons earlier this month.
Italian police were out in force again Friday with riot brigades, drones and helicopters visible in the skies above the Rome protest.
Their presence was heavy after protesters stormed Rome’s historic Colosseum on Saturday, while in the south, farmers and truckers have blockaded highways and ports to protest high fuel prices which have risen since the United States and Israel launched the war against Iran.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni , who has made law and order a key tenet of her administration, said she had “great respect” for peaceful protesters on X earlier this month.
But her right-wing government has since introduced tougher penalties for rioters, including financial liability for parents whose children take part in vandalism and looting.
“There is nothing revolutionary about vandalizing and stealing. Vandalism and theft are not protest, they are criminality,” Meloni said on social media after unveiling the legislation.
The government also said it would deploy 500 army troops alongside the police in Milan until the end of the year.
NBC News Chief Foreign Correspondent
Sara Monetta is a multimedia producer based in London.

articles.title_orig: Poland deploys riot police, as court chief’s ousting sparks crisis
articles.title_zh: Poland deploys riot police, as court chief’s ousting sparks crisis
articles.content_orig:
President Karol Nawrocki called off a visit to Africa in mid-flight, returning to Warsaw to deal with the turmoil at home
Poland’s President Karol Nawrocki called off a visit to Africa in mid-flight, as riot police deployed around the country’s constitutional court on Friday following the suspension of its chief justice in a battle between the centrist government and the nationalist right.
Dozens of police guarded the entrance to the court as followers of the opposition right-wing Law and Justice party (PiS) protested against the ousting of constitutional court president Bogdan Swieczkowski.
The court’s official social media account said there had been a “coup d’etat” and some demonstrators chanted “Tusk traitor”, as they condemned the government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

articles.title_orig: Trump says Iran wants to talk, predicts conflict will end 'very soon'
articles.title_zh: Trump says Iran wants to talk, predicts conflict will end 'very soon'
articles.content_orig:
Coverage for this event has ended.
A supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels of oil caught fire Friday after hitting a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s Revolutionary Guard said, according to state media.
It was the fourth oil tanker to suffer an explosion Friday after using unauthorized routes through the strait, the Guard said, according to The Associated Press.
Tehran has repeatedly said vessels must receive permission before traveling through the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran warned last month that vessels traveling through the strait without permission risked "destruction."
The Associated Press contributed to this report.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio met Friday with Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud to discuss regional issues, including Iran, Sudan and Yemen, the State Department said.
They met on the sidelines of the G20 foreign ministers' meeting in Atlanta.
"They discussed bilateral cooperation on a number of regional issues, including in Iran, Sudan, and Yemen," the State Department said in a statement.
"Secretary Rubio also signed the Expo 2030 participation contract, formalizing U.S. participation in Expo 2030 Riyadh, where we will showcase American innovation, expand opportunities for U.S. businesses, and strengthen our partnership with Saudi Arabia," the statement added.
Iran's political establishment is showing signs of divisions over how to end the country's prolonged conflict with the U.S. and Israel as diplomatic efforts intensify, according to Iran International .
Reformist and moderate figures have pushed for renewed negotiations with Washington, while conservatives and hardliners have emphasized military deterrence and maintaining Tehran's demands, the outlet reported.
The debate follows a reported call from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei to end the war, while maintaining that any agreement must meet Iran's conditions, according to Iran International.
President Masoud Pezeshkian has called for negotiations, arguing that prolonged uncertainty is hurting Iran's economy.
Hardliners, meanwhile, have argued that Tehran should strengthen its military position and economic resilience.
Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said Friday that President Donald Trump has been "very upfront" with Americans about the impact the war with Iran is having on fuel prices , calling the increase a "short-term consequence."
"If you also look at what the president has done for our energy industry, he is bringing down the price of gasoline and diesel," Leavitt said during an appearance on "The Story with Martha MacCallum."
"Of course, he's been very upfront with voters in Iowa and all across the country about what the war in Iran is doing," she said. "It's a short-term consequence. But overall, his energy policy will bring gas prices and diesel costs down again."
Leavitt contrasted Trump's energy agenda with Democrats' policies.
"If you look at it in contrast to what the Democrats want to do, they want to completely shut down and phase out our country from fossil fuels, which will jack up energy costs, which will not be good for anyone in rural America or anywhere in America," she said.
Yemen's government said Friday that Iran-aligned Houthis launched ballistic missile attacks targeting Aden International Airport and the presidential palace complex in the city.
A spokesperson for Yemen's armed forces said the Houthis targeted the airport and the Maashiq presidential palace complex, according to Reuters.
Officials did not immediately provide details on casualties or damage, or say whether the missiles struck their intended targets.
Reuters contributed to this report.
Streamer Hasan Piker compared pro-Israel Jewish voters in Michigan to the Ku Klux Klan during a livestream Thursday.
Piker made the comparison while discussing campaign volunteers for Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed canvassing a Jewish neighborhood outside Detroit.
He called it "the wildest door-knocking operation of all time," saying volunteers were trying to convince "one of the more Zionist, wealthy districts in the country to vote for a Muslim anti-Zionist."
"Brave soldiers — all of 'em," Piker said.
“This is the equivalent of going to that, like, Klan, KKK neighborhood to stump for like a Black candidate,” he said. “... The supremacist attitude underlying in their worldview is identical.”
He added, “If you are pro-Israel to the degree that you are making a big fuss about never voting for Abdul El-Sayed, a Muslim anti-Zionist, yes, it is the equivalent. ... It’s racial supremacy. It’s Jewish supremacy.”
Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned Friday that ongoing global crises threaten energy and food supplies, trade and freedom of navigation as G20 foreign ministers gathered in Atlanta.
"We are tasked, on behalf of the nations that we serve, to work together with one another to coordinate responses to emerging crises and to protect our shared interests," Rubio said in opening remarks, according to Reuters.
"We can help set the context for expanded geopolitical stability and the broader economic prosperity agenda that our leaders will tackle."
The meeting comes as the ongoing war with Iran has raised concerns about global energy supplies and shipping.
Reuters contributed to this report.
Germany's Foreign Office said Friday that most G20 nations agree that Iran must return to negotiations.
"Most of the [G20] share our view: [Iran] must come to the negotiating table, the [Houthis] must cease their attacks, and [Russia] must stop driving global [food security] towards collapse with its attacks in the Black Sea," the account wrote on X.
The statement came as G20 nations gathered amid heightened tensions in the Middle East.
President Donald Trump said Friday that Iran wants "to talk" as the war stretches into its eighth month.
"They want to talk. They keep talking," Trump told reporters.
The president claimed that Iran is struggling to pay its security forces as the conflict continues.
"Look, they're not paying their soldiers, they're not paying their police. They're, you know, they're in a lot of trouble," he said.
The president also described the conflict as "not a typical war" and said Washington is spending "very little money, relatively speaking."
Trump also defended the cost of the U.S. campaign, saying the money was spent "in order to get rid of a nuclear weapon," while arguing U.S. actions in Venezuela have more than offset the expense.
"Any money we've spent in Iran, we've more than made up for with what we did in Venezuela," he said.
The U.S. Embassy in Riyadh on Friday again warned Americans in Saudi Arabia to exercise extreme caution around airports amid ongoing Houthi attacks and travel disruptions.
In its latest security alert, the embassy reiterated that non-emergency U.S. government employees and their family members were ordered to leave Saudi Arabia effective Oct. 23 due to "safety risks."
"Iranian-supported Houthis have engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions. The hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly beyond that immediate area," the U.S. Embassy in Riyadh wrote on X.
U.S. citizens were also warned of potential attacks on airports, airspace closures, flight cancellations and other travel disruptions.
"Please take extreme caution if you choose to use airports in Saudi Arabia," the post added.
October saw the highest number of reported maritime incidents in the Strait of Hormuz region since the U.S.-Iran conflict began , according to data released by the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO).
The UKMTO report shows incidents across the Strait of Hormuz, Arabian Gulf and Gulf of Oman climbed to their highest monthly level in October, with 144 total events reported since Feb. 28.

articles.title_orig: Traffic Control Errors Caused Spain’s Deadly Train Crash, Official Says
articles.title_zh: Traffic Control Errors Caused Spain’s Deadly Train Crash, Official Says
articles.content_orig:
Individuals from as many as 27 different countries may have died in this week’s high-speed train collision in Spain, the country’s prime minister said Friday, as the process to identify victims continued.
The deadly crash happened Wednesday after one train plowed into another near the town of Urda, in Toledo province, on the high-speed line that connects Madrid and Seville, killing at least 69 people and injuring over 100 others. Authorities say the incident was caused by both computer system failure and apparent human error.
One of the trains, operated by Spain’s national rail company Renfe, crashed into a stationary train operated by the private company Iryo, at a time when all rail traffic in the area was disrupted due to a problem with the LZB train management safety system.
It was the third deadly incident on the country’s rail network this year following a major crash in January in Córdoba province, in which more than 40 people died, and a crash near Barcelona that killed a train driver.
Spain’s Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has announced an official mourning period from Thursday until Saturday.
Spain’s transportation minister, Óscar Puente, said a computer system failure led to an issue with the safety system along a 63-kilometer (40-mile) stretch of track causing all trains in the area to be stopped automatically.
At that point, the state-owned company that manages Spain’s railways, ADIF, took manual command of the system and a decision was made to allow the high-speed Renfe train to continue southbound along the tracks despite a red light.
The Renfe train was authorized to proceed without any speed restrictions due to an erroneous order from a train controller. As a result, Puente said that between 8:36 a.m. and 8:52 a.m. local time, it resumed traveling at about 124 miles per hour, eventually colliding with the stationary Iryo train.
“There was a red signal prohibiting movement, yet the train was authorized to proceed,” the transportation minister said at a press conference on Wednesday. “It is a decision made under inexplicable circumstances.”
Following Puente’s comments, Spanish trade union CSIF called on the transport minister to resign, saying: “We demand that the Government respect the investigation and the presumption of innocence for the head of traffic at ADIF.” CNN has approached Spain’s transport ministry for comment.
Audio recordings published in Spanish media reveal conversations between the train drivers and the controller in the moments leading up to the crash. The recordings appear to show that the Renfe train was given clearance to move, with the controller telling it to continue onward at “normal operation.”
In another recording, the driver of the Iryo train involved in the crash also receives the instruction to resume “normal operation.” Minutes later the driver reports that she is unable to restart her train and it is currently not moving.
The collision occurred while the Renfe train was traveling at a speed estimated to be between 160 km/h (nearly 100 mph) and 200 km/h (around 124 mph), according to AITAT, the independent body responsible for investigating the incident.
Passengers told CNN that the moment of the crash was “very chaotic,” and people were immediately thrown out of their seats and on top of one another inside the carriages.
One surviving passenger said that three of the train cars in particular “were in terrible shape.”
“One was on fire, in another there were people trapped and crying,” said the passenger, who declined to give her name. “And then in the main one (impacted) – there were people buried under debris.”
In total there were 151 passengers on the Iryo train and 393 passengers on the Renfe train, according to the latest update from the regional government of Castilla and La Mancha.
Of the 110 injured people who were taken to the hospital, 60 have been released, according to an update from the regional government on Thursday.
Puente added that there will be a full investigation into the incident.
Little is known at this stage regarding the identity of the victims. Identification efforts are ongoing while emergency staff continue to comb through the wrecked carriages at the crash site, where rescuers and cranes worked through the night under floodlights.
The Spanish Civil Guard announced that it has opened four offices in different Spanish cities to swiftly identify the victims of the crash. The Civil Guard said that the DNA of families is being gathered to aid this process. 67 missing persons reports have been filed in the wake of the accident, the force confirmed to CNN.
One mother, Rosario, told CNN she had provided DNA samples to help find her missing 32-year-old son, Francisco José, who was on board one of the trains. Rosario said her son had also been about to board one of the trains involved in the Adamuz crash in January, but eventually decided to buy a ticket for a later journey instead.
The Civil Guard announced that one of its own officers lost his life in Wednesday’s crash. Naming the victim as José Manuel, the police force offered its “deepest condolences” to his family, friends, and colleagues. A former Spanish minister, Fátima Báñez, was also killed, her People’s Party (PP) confirmed on Thursday.
In the wake of the crash more than 500 emergency personnel were deployed to assist with rescue operations, Spain’s interior ministry said, as well as at least three helicopters and several drones.
Authorities removed passengers without serious injuries away from the scene by bus. The evacuated passengers included citizens of multiple nationalities, including Spain, Brazil and elsewhere, according to CNN’s producer at the scene. The US State Department has said “several” Americans were injured in the train collision.
Portugal’s foreign ministry confirmed a Portuguese national died in the crash, adding that he had been a crew member on one of the trains involved.
A 24-year-old Spanish athlete is also thought to have lost her life. Long jumper Julieta Gallego competed for the Madrid-based track and field club AD Sprint. The Royal Spanish Athletics Federation (RFEF) announced her death, while her club said they were “heartbroken.”
Two Italian citizens remain missing, according to Italy’s foreign ministry, while another has safely made contact with Consular services.
Sánchez has said that the Spanish government will provide compensation for families of the victims.
The crash on Wednesday happened about 130 miles from the site of the January train disaster near the town of Adamuz, along the same high-speed rail route that runs between Madrid and Seville.
However, the cause of the train crash earlier this year was markedly different. That collision involved one train derailing due to a break in the track and crossing onto an adjacent track, according to Spain’s public broadcaster RTVE.
Prior to the Adamuz train disaster, Spain’s train drivers’ union, SEMAF, had raised concerns about high speeds causing vibrations and subsequent wear and tear along high-speed railway lines, a source from the union told CNN at the time.
Spain’s train drivers held a pre-planned nationwide strike Thursday to call for stronger safety measures.
Speaking to reporters during the strike, SEMAF Secretary General Diego Martín called for a “rigorous and independent investigation” into the crash and criticized the leaking of audio from the control center as “alarming, disrespectful and irresponsible.”
A third crash this year near Barcelona – which happened days after the Adamuz train disaster – involved a commuter train derailing on a day of heavy rainfall. That crash killed the driver and injuring dozens of passengers, according to the regional government of Catalonia at the time.
The successive incidents have raised concerns about Spain’s railway infrastructure, computer systems and the maintenance of both.

articles.title_orig: He questioned Thailand's monarchy dressed as Harry Potter. Now he's in jail for 34 years
articles.title_zh: He questioned Thailand's monarchy dressed as Harry Potter. Now he's in jail for 34 years
articles.content_orig:
Even before they come through the door, you can hear the prisoners walking towards the courtroom, the shackles round their ankles clinking with each step.
The five who walk into the courtroom are familiar with the routine; they are facing multiple criminal prosecutions and have spent much of the past five years going back and forth to court.
One of them, a small, bespectacled man with greying hair, opens his arms to hold his three-year-old son, who has been brought to court by his partner to see him.
This is Arnon Nampa, a 42-year-old human rights lawyer. His offence was to call for Thailand's powerful monarchy to be scrutinised and held accountable. He did this dressed as the eponymous young wizard at a Harry Potter-themed demonstration in central Bangkok in 2020.
On Friday a court in Bangkok sentenced him to two years and eight months for violating Thailand's lèse majesté law, or article 112, under which more people have been jailed for perceived insults against the royal family than in all the other countries that have such laws combined.
This is just one out of 14 cases brought against Arnon under the same charge, bringing the cumulative sentence he has received so far to more than 34 years. The verdict in two cases is still pending.
"To me, this isn't a surprise," he later told reporters. "If the country was more open, we would be able to talk about these issues freely."
The past six years have seen the most extensive use of lèse majesté in Thai history, in response to unprecedented student protests in 2020 which for the first time called for a public discussion of the role of the monarchy. Two hundred and ninety-four people, including 20 under the age of 18, have been prosecuted, receiving prison sentences of up to 50 years. Dozens of them are still on trial.
Most of those charged under this law are denied bail and kept in jail, even though their court cases can last several years. The standard defence of the law given by Thai officials is that it "reflects the culture and history of Thailand, where the monarchy is one of the main pillars of the nation, highly revered by the majority of Thai people".
Article 112 of the Thai criminal code simply reads, "Whoever defames, insults or threatens the King, the Queen, the Heir-apparent or the Regent, shall be punished with imprisonment of three to 15 years."
In practice, though, the law has been interpreted to cover a much wider range of comment about the monarchy, and a much wider range of figures. Saying anything negative about any member of the royal family, about the institution of the monarchy, even about long deceased kings, or in one case, the king's dog, has resulted in prosecutions.
"If you ask me what the text of the law says, I can tell you," says Akarachai Chaimaneekarakate, assistant director of Thai Lawyers for Human Rights, which helps defend those accused of breaking it. "If you ask me how the courts interpret the words "defame" or "insult", I don't think I can give you a definition, because it's so ambiguous, it's so vague. Even questioning the law itself, for example, can constitute lèse majesté under Section 112."
From his cell in the Bangkok Remand Prison, where he has been for the last three years, Arnon has been writing to his young daughter and son.
"Dear Pran and Karl, my beloved children," one of his letters reads, "The winter wind has not only brought us cool weather, but also brings back stories from the past. I miss the time we travelled outside Bangkok that first winter after Karl came into this world. It was such a magical time for me. I shall miss it every winter I spend here until I regain my freedom."
Hearings like the one Arnon attended weeks before Friday's verdict are the only times he has seen Karl since he was a baby.
Karl is shy at first, but soon he's happy to be picked up and shown off to the other prisoners. His 10-year-old sister Pran sometimes visits their father in prison, and often draws and paints him.
But Arnon and Lookwa, his partner, think Karl is too young to visit. For now, Karl thinks the court is just where his dad works. A group of supporters has come too, filling the little courtroom. They mingle cheerfully with the prisoners, laughing and exchanging gossip before the judges walk in to start the hearing. It is an improbably informal setting for men facing one of the most feared charges in Thailand.
The effect of the law has been to smother any public discussion about the monarchy. Until six years ago, opinions on it were only ever whispered in private. In one notorious case a taxi driver was jailed because a passenger reported what he had said while riding in his cab.
That changed on 3 August 2020.
That year younger Thais had become increasingly frustrated with the conservative government led by coup-leader Gen Prayuth Chan-ocha. The year before millions had given their votes to a new party, Future Forward, which promised sweeping reforms, but in February 2020, the Constitutional Court dissolved the party on a technicality. The arrival of the Covid pandemic prevented any protests for three months, but as infections in Thailand started to fall, students began holding rallies calling for an end to the military's role in politics. Arnon Nampa argued this did not go far enough.
In the garb of Harry Potter, he gave a speech saying it was time to talk about the opaque power and wealth of the monarchy. He criticised King Vajiralongkorn's decision to take personal control of the vast assets held by the Crown Property Bureau, and over important units of the army.
In a single speech Arnon shattered a taboo which had hung over Thai society for the whole of its modern history. For the rest of that year the student-led protests continued, with increasingly bold demands for changes to the monarchy.
At the time, the use of the lèse majesté law had been suspended for three years. Sources close to the palace have in the past acknowledged that the negative publicity generated by lèse majesté convictions might do more harm than good.
But the protests forced a hasty reassessment. From the end of 2020 prosecutions under the law restarted and accelerated. Dozens of young activists have fled into exile to avoid being jailed.
One of them is Supitcha "Melinn" Chailom. The 24-year-old from Chiang Mai in northern Thailand lives in Montreal, a fugitive from four 112 charges which have been filed against her.
She was an 18-year-old school girl when she stood up and made a speech at a protest in Chiang Mai University, just three weeks after Arnon Nampa's call for reform of the monarchy.
A local photographer captured the moment she raised her hand in the three-finger Hunger Games salute, eliciting loud cheers from the crowd. It became one of the defining images of the protests, and propelled Melinn to nationwide fame.
She travelled up and down the country as one of the leading voices in the movement, demanding changes to Thailand's old-fashioned education system, conducting polls on what people thought of the monarchy.
"I love playing games, and I dreamed of being a game designer," she told me from Canada. But her parents did not approve.
"I felt that, as a young person, I could not question, or have a discussion with people older than me. The monarchy gave me the same vibe."
In November 2020 Melinn joined a protest in the southern city of Hat Yai, where she gave a speech comparing the royal treatment given to the king's dog with that of ordinary people. Nine months later the police delivered a summons to her home charging her with lèse majesté.
"It was a shock. I wasn't expecting it because I only talked about the dog. It was during Covid when the police came to my home with the summons, so they knew my parents would be there with me. They tried to stay calm, but I nearly lost my mind."
Her family tried to persuade her to co-operate with the authorities, to admit her wrongdoing. But Melinn refused.

articles.title_orig: Meta’s Rating Outlook Cut to Negative by S&P on AI Spending
articles.title_zh: Meta’s Rating Outlook Cut to Negative by S&P on AI Spending
articles.content_orig:
Meta Platforms released its third-quarter earnings report on Oct. 21. Here’s Morningstar’s take on Meta’s earnings and stock.
Meta reported third-quarter results that included 26% top-line growth to $64.6 billion and adjusted operating margins contracting 500 basis points to 35%. Rising artificial-intelligence-related costs continue to drive the margin contraction. Meta expects fourth-quarter sales to grow 21%-27%.
Why it matters: Investors have been concerned about Meta’s ability to monetize its AI investments. We see momentum in core advertising, as well as adoption of Muse (both on the consumer and enterprise side), as early signals that the firm’s AI playbook is working.
The bottom line: Shares are down 12% since the report, as a $25 billion equity raise has stoked concerns about the sustainability of AI investments, overshadowing otherwise solid results. We maintain our $850 per share fair value estimate for wide-moat Meta and view the stock as undervalued.
The following are excerpts from Morningstar’s company report on Meta.
With its 4-star rating, we believe Meta’s stock is moderately undervalued compared with our long-term fair value estimate of $850 per share, which implies a 2026 adjusted price/earnings multiple of 26 times and an enterprise value/adjusted EBITDA multiple of 13 times.
We forecast Meta’s sales growing at a 22% compound annual growth rate for the next five years, spearheaded primarily by an increase in average revenue per user, with user growth also chipping in. On advertising, we believe Meta has a strong monetization opportunity ahead of it in Asia and the rest of the world.
We additionally expect Meta to leverage its AI data center buildout by either renting out excess capacity to AI labs or selling intelligence to external customers via Meta API and Muse Code. We expect a combination of these businesses to grow from practically $0 in 2026 to $40 billion by 2030.
Read more about Meta Platforms’ fair value estimate.
We believe Meta merits a wide economic moat rating due to the firm’s intangible assets and the potent network effect around its Family of Apps business. While the firm’s Reality Labs segment continues to hemorrhage cash, we believe the FoA’s strong competitive advantages will likely allow the firm to generate returns over its cost of capital over the next two decades.
In our view, the firm could leverage AI to improve its ad tech business, improving advertiser ROI and encouraging more ad dollars to be spent on its platform. Further, we see potential long-term opportunities for the firm to sell excess compute to external labs as well as sell its models to external customers via Meta Enterprise or Meta API. One important caveat is that Meta has no track record of running an enterprise business.
We believe Meta’s Reality Labs business merits a no moat rating. While the firm’s investments in metaverse and virtual/augmented reality could lead to profitable growth in the future, the segment continues to burn capital for Meta.
Read more about Meta Platforms’ economic moat.
We view Meta’s financial position as solid. The firm closed fiscal 2025 with cash and cash equivalents of $82 billion, more than offsetting its debt balance of $59 billion.
While the firm’s investments in AI stand to increase its capital expenditure considerably over the next few years, the advertising business remains a cash-generating machine, with cash flows from this business continuing to fund the AI investments.
Read more about Meta Platforms’ financial strength.
We assign Meta an Uncertainty Rating of High. We believe the company’s investments in unprofitable ventures such as generative AI and Reality Labs add a layer of uncertainty around its business, even as its large and stable advertising business continues to generate substantial cash flows in our forecast.
The firm’s high dependence on user behavior data represents an environmental, social, and governance risk. If it fails to maintain adequate data privacy and security, Meta’s advertising business will likely suffer. Also, the broader impact of social media on its users’ mental health, especially that of teenagers, is also a pertinent ESG risk for Meta.

articles.title_orig: Apple Alerts Stores to iPhone Duo's Display Cracking Issue
articles.title_zh: Apple Alerts Stores to iPhone Duo's Display Cracking Issue
articles.content_orig:
In a memo shared with Apple Stores and Apple Authorized Service Providers this week, and later obtained by MacRumors , Apple provided technicians with guidance on how to diagnose and address the iPhone Duo's inner display cracking issue.
If a customer reports the issue, Apple advised technicians to inspect the iPhone Duo and repair or replace it in accordance with their standard procedures. While the instructions themselves are straightforward, the fact that Apple issued an internal memo suggests the issue is widespread enough to warrant official guidance.
Apple's memo said the issue affects a small number of iPhone Duo units, which is consistent with what it said in a public statement on Monday.
"We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units," said Apple, in a statement shared with MacRumors . If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for a replacement." You can get support on Apple's website or by calling 1-800-APL-CARE in the U.S. and Canada.
Apple said most iPhone Duo units are not susceptible to this issue and that impacted units appear to exhibit the defects rather quickly after usage.
Apple said there is no iPhone Duo recall, and the company has yet to launch a public-facing repair program on its website for this issue.
Almost immediately after the iPhone Duo began arriving to customers a week ago, a handful of early adopters reported that the device's inner display had cracked , resulting in lines appearing down the middle and towards the right side of the screen.
The electronics repair website iFixit completed an iPhone Duo teardown and said that the issue is likely related to a defective hinge on affected units. However, Apple has yet to comment on the underlying cause of the issue.

articles.title_orig: Consensus looks elusive at G20 talks after European objections to Russia cancel group photo
articles.title_zh: Consensus looks elusive at G20 talks after European objections to Russia cancel group photo
articles.content_orig:
Marco Rubio pulls plug on traditional photo op at meeting of foreign ministers after about one-third of countries threaten boycott
The traditional “family photo” to open the G20 foreign ministers’ meeting has been abruptly cancelled in the US after a host of nations – including Australia and the UK – refused to appear beside the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov.
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, pulled the plug after several European officials, the UK and Australia made it known they would boycott or walk out of the snapshot that often kicks off such international gatherings.
Rubio still opened the talks in Atlanta with an appeal for unity on the issues that threaten international security and trade.
“We are in a critical moment,” Rubio told his colleagues. “We are facing a series of interconnected economic and geopolitical crises.”
About one-third of countries at the talks made it known they would not appear beside any Russian representatives.
European Union nations had made clear they would boycott any photo with the Russians. “In no case will there be a family photo with European partners and Mr Lavrov together because … there is no normality with Russia,” Germany’s foreign affairs minister, Johann Wadephul, warned ahead of Friday’s session.
The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, promised similar. “We do not engage in that way with the Russians and have not for a number of years,” he said.
During the meeting’s opening session, Australia’s foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, condemned Russia’s invasion of Ukraine as brutal and unjustified - in front of Lavrov - saying Russia’s illegal war had affected international markets and worsened global food security.
A spokesperson for Wong said Australia supported the US decision to cancel the group photo. “Australia has been clear and consistent: we will not normalise Russia’s brutal and illegal invasion of Ukraine.
“Our focus at the G20 remains on the important work before us and addressing the challenges facing the global economy.”
The schism in Atlanta is yet further evidence of the rupture caused by the Trump administration’s attempt to reintegrate Russia and its isolated president, Vladimir Putin, into the international community despite Putin’s ongoing war against Ukraine.
Diplomats who attended the opening session described it as cordial but said Russia’s position on Ukraine is unyielding – as is its opposition to Poland’s membership in the G20.
Those disagreements, which also include the Trump administration’s not inviting G20 member South Africa over the objections of others, will probably prevent the foreign ministers from producing a joint communique when the meetings wrap up on Saturday, participants said.
That did not surprise the Polish deputy prime minister and foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, representing his country at its first time as a guest at a G20 meeting.
“We have wars going on and we have participants in those wars around the table, so it’s very difficult to agree a common line,” he told reporters.
Several participants, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the closed-door talks, said all had agreed to try to overcome their differences despite the long odds and to work to make next month’s G20 leaders’ summit hosted by the president, Donald Trump, in Florida a success.
Ukraine, which is not a G20 member but was invited to attend previous meetings, was not invited this year, with US officials saying it was a deliberate choice to include only formal members of the group. Poland, not a member, is seeking formal membership with US support.
But missing from the invitation list was South Africa, a G20 founding member and the only African country in the group. South Africa is embroiled in several bitter disputes with the Trump administration, and when it chaired the G20 last year, top US officials, including Trump and Rubio, shunned the meetings it hosted.
“We have consistently maintained that our nonparticipation is not voluntary,” Phindile Kunene, a spokesperson for the South African international relations minister, Ronald Lamola, said.

articles.title_zh: Wall Street abandons ship after gold sinks below $3,900/oz, Main Street maintains bullish majority bias as midterms, payrolls loom
articles.content_orig:
Kitco NEWS has a diverse team of journalists reporting on the economy, stock markets, commodities, cryptocurrencies, mining and metals with accuracy and objectivity. Our goal is to help people make informed market decisions through in-depth reporting, daily market roundups, interviews with prominent industry figures, comprehensive coverage (often exclusive) of important industry events and analyses of market-affecting developments.
(Kitco News) – Gold prices suffered another sharp weekly decline, as an early recovery gave way to heavy selling after the Federal Reserve maintained its hawkish stance, stronger U.S. economic data reinforced expectations for further tightening, and Friday's technology-led equity rout triggered widespread liquidation across precious metals.
Spot gold kicked off the week trading at $3,994.95 per ounce on Sunday evening, and the yellow metal initially pushed higher as bargain-hunting emerged following the previous week's selloff below $4,000. The recovery gathered momentum Tuesday as Treasury yields eased and the U.S. dollar softened, carrying gold back above $4,050 ahead of Wednesday's Federal Reserve policy decision. After the Fed voted 10-2 to hold interest rates steady at 3.75% to 4.00%, with two policymakers dissenting in favor of another 25-basis-point hike, spot prices ultimately set their weekly high at $4,082.50 per ounce just before the equity close on Wednesday, before sellers regained control.
Gold came under renewed pressure Thursday after stronger-than-expected third-quarter GDP growth and elevated core PCE inflation reinforced expectations that further monetary tightening could be necessary. The metal slipped back toward $4,000 as the dollar remained supported, despite some relief from easing Treasury yields and lower oil prices.
Selling accelerated dramatically on Friday as a sharp decline in technology stocks, driven by growing concerns over returns on artificial intelligence investment, triggered broader market liquidations. Gold broke decisively below $4,000 and continued falling alongside silver and other precious metals, as forced selling and expectations for another Fed rate hike overwhelmed safe-haven demand. Spot gold ultimately set its weekly low of $3,870.25 per ounce late Friday afternoon – its weakest level in more than a year – and was trading only a few dollars above that level heading into the close.
The latest Kitco News Weekly Gold Survey showed Wall Street bulls abandoning ship after gold sank below $3,900, while Main Street maintained a narrow bullish majority bias despite the yellow metal’s price rout.
“Gold’s shine has dulled,” said Marc Chandler, managing director at Bannockburn Global Forex. “The yellow metal was near $4700 as recently as late August. The one caveat is that the once-more precious metal is below the lower Bollinger Band (two standard deviations below the 20-day moving average. Still, there does not appear to have been a capitulation trade, and assuming a push to new lows for the year, I suspect gold can fall into the $3750-$3850 range.”
“Lower,” said Adam Button, head of currency strategy at investingLive. “It's a big week with the midterms and the potential resumption of the Iran war, but I fear that Trump could lash out and escalate, leading to a severe risk-off trade.”
“I am bearish on Gold for the coming week,” said Colin Cieszynski, chief market strategist at SIA Wealth Management. “Technically, the breakdown below $4,000 is significant.”
“Unchanged,” said Rich Checkan, president and COO of Asset Strategies International. “I see competing influences this coming week. Renewed strikes on oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz may bring retaliation soon after U.S. mid-term elections. That should push oil prices higher and stoke inflation concerns… putting downward pressure on gold. But if Democrats make gains in the mid-term elections, it may very well drive uneasy Republicans to the safety and protection of gold.”
“I would treat every drop in gold prices as an opportunity to buy well,” Checkan added.
Daniel Pavilonis, senior commodities broker at StoneX Group, told Kitco News that now that gold and silver have broken near-term critical support, the precious metals may be in for a longer and deeper correction, and gold will need some indication of easing monetary policy to resume the upward trajectory of the last couple of years.
“We're still seeing some inflation,” he said. “We're seeing equities sell off. We're seeing commodities have come off, except for some of the energy sector.
Pavilonis said the market is in the midst of an unwind. “If you're looking at the charts, they don't look so hot... If you're just looking at this from a technical standpoint, not any fundamentals, it looks like we could go lower.”
As for how low the precious metals could slide, Pavilonis said the metals could be in for a deep pullback before sustained buying resumes.
“I could see silver getting as low as the high $30s,” he said. “I could see gold getting as low as somewhere around $3,000. I think it's very likely to happen into the first quarter of next year, and then maybe just base out for a little while, and then possibly move higher.”
Pavilonis said he’s seen this time and time again. “What happened the last few times when silver hit $50, when gold spikes up? We sell off afterward,” he said. “The party is over. The themes that we [saw at the early 2026 highs], the same headlines, the same stories… because of inflation, because of this or that. People need to rationalize why it went up so much. But if you go back into the archives and look at news around 1980 – before people realized it was the Hunt brothers, which was part of the story – but it was the same thing: ‘We're running out of silver, we're running out of gold, the exchanges are low, warehouses are low, inventories… And people are buying, and so you’ve got to go out and buy some gold, go out and buy some silver!’ There were almost identical New York Times articles being written about silver and gold in the run-up to 1980.”
“Now I think that anybody from the move to the upside that hasn't been stopped out, or is holding on the physical side, It's time to hedge,” he said. “You want to start collaring around positions. You want to start collaring and capitalizing on it. Because if it does go lower, then there's ways to mitigate that, put yourself in the right position where you can accumulate more. That's what I would be thinking about right now.”
Pavilonis said that if we see further liquidations across financial markets, he expects to see more selling of gold as well.
“We have this rationale to buy and hold onto the metals,” he said. “I think in the long term you're going to be right. But in the short term, the thesis can be wrong, so it's time to maybe even hedge a little bit further if you haven't already.”
This week, 16 analysts participated in the Kitco News Gold Survey, with Wall Street’s bullish belief all but evaporating after gold couldn’t hold $3,900. Only one expert, or 6%, expected to see gold prices gain ground during the week ahead, while 10, representing 63%, saw the yellow metal declining further. The remaining five analysts, 31% of the total, said they couldn’t predict gold’s direction, or expected sideways trading next week.
Meanwhile, 184 votes were cast in Kitco’s online poll, with Main Street investors once again more bullish than their professional counterparts despite gold’s steep selloff. 98 retail traders, or 53%, looked for gold prices to rise next week, while 56 others, or 30%, predicted the yellow metal would lose further ground. The remaining 30 investors, representing 16% of the total, expected to see price consolidation during the week ahead.
Next week will feature top-tier economic data and geopolitical risk events for investors to navigate, with the U.S. midterm elections and October’s nonfarm payrolls report the most significant of a raft of market-movers.

articles.title_orig: China’s Fourth Aircraft Carrier Could Arrive as Soon as Next Year
articles.title_zh: China’s Fourth Aircraft Carrier Could Arrive as Soon as Next Year
articles.content_orig:
By ELINA SHIRAZI, US SENIOR POLITICAL REPORTER
Published: 13:43 EDT, 30 October 2026 | Updated: 18:12 EDT, 30 October 2026
A dramatic surge in military tension has taken center stage as President Trump ordered a third US aircraft carrier to the Middle East – all while making cryptic claims that the standoff will soon reach its conclusion.
US Central Command confirmed that bringing three aircraft carrier strike groups into the Middle East represents the largest US naval surge in the region since the 2003 invasion of Iraq .
Trump voiced confidence today that the conflict would dissipate, though he provided no specific timeline or strategy for how that outcome would be secured.
'It's going to get wrapped up soon,' Trump stated during an interview with a Kansas City radio station. 'We need a guarantee there'll never be a nuclear weapon.'
The remarks comes as questions surrounding Trump's domestic campaign itinerary arise, with the President rescheduling several canceled rallies over the weekend.
Vice President JD Vance also canceled a scheduled Friday press briefing in St. Cloud, Minnesota , focused on the administration's 'War on Fraud.'
Officials have not provided a reason for the cancellation.
Recent reports suggest the administration is laying the groundwork for a fresh wave of aggressive military strikes if Iranian leaders refuse to sign an agreement.
The aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln is pictured
During campaign appearances, he has argued that hostilities will wrap up shortly following the midterms, provided the GOP retains control of Congress
Despite initiating the war in February expecting a rapid surrender from Iran's weakened regime, Trump has continuously maintained that the conflict will draw to a close, even while combat intensifies and global economic damage continues to mount.
This has led to voter dissatisfaction across both parties ahead of the midterm elections.
During campaign appearances, he has argued that hostilities will wrap up shortly following the midterms, provided the GOP retains control of Congress.
Two US officials report that the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit are scheduled to arrive in the Middle East by late November.
Upon arrival, the Roosevelt will operate alongside the USS George H.W. Bush, which deployed in April, and the USS George Washington, which arrived in August as a replacement for the USS Abraham Lincoln.
Meanwhile, the nation's highest–ranking Middle East commander has reportedly briefed Trump on potential strike scenarios regarding Iran.
Admiral Brad Cooper visited the White House on Thursday with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and General Dan Caine, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, the Wall Street Journal reports.
As Trump evaluates strategy options for resuming military action against Iran, the discussion with cabinet officials included potential plans for maintaining the ongoing regional blockade.
Following a high-level White House meeting involving military leadership and Vice President Vance, Hegseth removed Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia from his role as top strategist for the Joint Chiefs.
Sylvia's removal comes amid allegations that he leaked classified intelligence regarding the wars in Iran and Ukraine.

articles.title_orig: Mass protests sweep Italy during nationwide strike
articles.title_zh: Mass protests sweep Italy during nationwide strike
articles.content_orig:
ROME — Tens of thousands of people took to the streets of Rome, Milan and other Italian cities Friday as part of nationwide demonstrations against the cost of living and high military spending.
The demonstrations were largely peaceful but an NBC News crew saw police use a water cannon on protestors and groups of police charging to disperse protestors in Rome on Friday night.
After several weeks of violent protests in Italy and throughout Europe , more widespread disruption is expected after the Unione Sindacale di Base (USB) and other trade unions called on workers in both the public and private sectors to strike and protest.
The demonstrations in Italy appear to have been partly inspired by those in France , where some of the worst rioting in decades erupted in cities across the country after student protests about the state of education in the country evolved into wider actions about the cost of living and social security.
Elsewhere in Europe, a huge encampment of tents has occupied a square in Madrid since late last month, and thousands of people in Portugal have taken to the streets in the city of Lisbon. Tear gas and water cannons were also used on black-clad protesters in Brussels.
In Rome, many waved communist and Palestinian flags, as well as signs against the Iran war. Some let off pink smoke bombs. There was a jovial mood among the demonstrators as they lined up before the march, as has often been the case early on at previous protests, only for violence to break out later.
Protesters storm the Colosseum in Rome
Giovanna Di Matteo, a member of the left-wing Potere al Popolo! party, said she was protesting against the government that “did nothing for the people of this country.”
The government had spent money on the military “while they cut on welfare, they cut on services and people cannot reach the end of the month,” she said. “They have no money for their houses, they have no money for gasoline and everything.”
Luca, a 20-year-old medical student said the protesters felt they were “still not being heard, that everything is still the same,” and the government didn’t “care about our voice, about our voices, and about the future of this nation that is our nation.”
“We have been completely screwed by the fact that the wages do not keep up on inflation and the wages in general do not keep up with the cost of living,” added Luca, who asked to have his last name withheld out of fear of repercussions from law enforcement.
Major demonstrations also took place in other cities and towns across Italy.
They came after a number of protests in recent weeks have turned violent. Groups of masked protesters looted stores in Milan and elsewhere and threw projectiles at police, who responded with tear gas and water cannons earlier this month.
Italian police were out in force again Friday with riot brigades, drones and helicopters visible in the skies above the Rome protest.
Their presence was heavy after protesters stormed Rome’s historic Colosseum on Saturday, while in the south, farmers and truckers have blockaded highways and ports to protest high fuel prices which have risen since the United States and Israel launched the war against Iran.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni , who has made law and order a key tenet of her administration, said she had “great respect” for peaceful protesters on X earlier this month.
But her right-wing government has since introduced tougher penalties for rioters, including financial liability for parents whose children take part in vandalism and looting.
“There is nothing revolutionary about vandalizing and stealing. Vandalism and theft are not protest, they are criminality,” Meloni said on social media after unveiling the legislation.
The government also said it would deploy 500 army troops alongside the police in Milan until the end of the year.
NBC News Chief Foreign Correspondent
Sara Monetta is a multimedia producer based in London.

As OpenAI’s buying spree squeezes the world’s supply of RAM, its CEO explains why he needs so much.﻿
Asked about supply chain shortages, like the ongoing RAM shortage , OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in an interview that it’s “terrible” to have RAM in personal PCs instead of data centers. During his appearance on the Cheeky Pint podcast, where he also commented on AI’s impact on math , Altman said:
“A lot of people want local inference. And somehow, they assume that the problem is solved now because we are going to have open-source models, we’re going to be able to run them on our computers, and so we’re not going to need all the stuff in the data center.
But from a global allocation perspective, actually, it’s quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world’s limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer and being used five percent of the time.
You want maximum utilization in the cloud if you’re trying to deal with this very supply constrained environment. And somehow everyone’s— many people’s intuition is the opposite of that.”
Whether Altman meant your gaming PC or developers working with something like the Surface RTX Spark Dev Box or the new touchscreen MacBook Pro , the outcome is the same. Right now, memory companies Samsung and SK Hynix have long term deals with cloud service operators and projects like OpenAI’s Stargate that have reserved much of the world’s RAM output over the next few years. And the billions they’re willing to lay out for chips is why the laptops, phones, and other tech you use are getting more expensive right now.

Polish president Karol Nawrocki turned back his plane en route to Senegal on Friday as the country’s top court was thrown into chaos after its president was suspended.
Police and protesters clashed outside the Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw after the government suspended its two senior justices and moved to bring criminal charges against them. Reports suggest riot police were deployed on Friday evening as demonstrators supporting the Law and Order (PiS) party, who oppose the government, threw objects at officers.
"At a moment like this, the President must be in Poland . I am cutting short my flight to Senegal. I am returning," Mr Nawrocki, who is backed by the PiS, said on X.
The tribunal ⁠said on its website that the court's president, Bogdan Swieczkowski, ​had ⁠been suspended on Friday.
A ‌long-running political dispute over the Constitutional Tribunal has effectively paralysed the institution.
Earlier this year, Mr Nawrocki, an ally of ‌Poland's former nationalist government of the Law ‌and Justice or PiS party, refused to swear in three of six judges nominated by parliament, while Swieczkowski, who was a deputy ⁠justice minister under PiS, declined to allow judges elected by the current parliamentary majority to assume their duties.
Restoring the rule of law is the government's duty, prime minister Donald Tusk said on X later on Friday.
“Restoring the rule of law is our obligation,” prime minister Tusk wrote on X on Friday evening. “After years of lawlessness under PiS this is a difficult process, sometimes painful and it requires decisive action. There is no other way.”
Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek told ‌reporters he has requested the ⁠lifting of the immunities of Swieczkowski and his deputy ⁠for failing to fulfill their duties by preventing judges from performing their ‌work.
PiS politicians, ​including leader Jaroslaw Kaczynski, said Tusk's ‌government was carrying out a ​coup on the tribunal.

Ukrainian president says Kyiv’s battlefield ⁠position strongest ⁠in some ​time. What we know on day 1,708
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said Ukrainian forces are retaking territory through a series of offensives , adding Kyiv’s battlefield ⁠position was the strongest it had been ⁠in some ​time. The Ukrainian president, citing ⁠a report by senior commanders, noted for the first time the “Veles” operation using pipelines in Ukraine’s northeast. He also referred to an air assault operation in ⁠eastern Ukraine and the “Vivaldi” operation further to the north, designed to prevent Russian advances in ​key areas.
The leaders of Finland and Norway phoned Russian president Vladimir Putin on Tuesday to urge him to end the war in Ukraine. The call by Finnish president Alexander Stubb and Norwegian prime minister Jonas Gahr Stoere was an attempt to ⁠influence the diplomatic process after US president Donald ⁠Trump stunned allies by agreeing to buy Russian diesel, plunging ties with Ukraine to their lowest point in 18 months.
While a localised ceasefire appears to holding in Ukraine’s south, Russian strikes damaged a university campus and Kyiv’s important Southern Bridge overnight , in what Zelenskyy described as “a serious escalation” against ​Ukrainian logistics. A Ukrainian military source told Reuters that Russia ‌had hit the bridge with four Iskander ​ballistic missiles. Zelenskyy said energy facilities, logistics and infrastructure in ​10 other regions had also been attacked overnight.
Kyiv plans to allocate 1 billion hryvnias ($22 ⁠million) to build water crossings over the River Dnipro that divides ⁠the capital into two ⁠parts , ​the city’s mayor has said, as Russia escalates its attacks on ⁠bridges.
Romanian president Nicusor Dan has called an alleged Russian sabotage plot last month a “grave violation” of the Nato member’s sovereignty and security . Dan’s remarks on Tuesday came a day after the Romanian intelligence service said it identified a Russia-coordinated “sabotage network” linked to a fire in central Brasov County last month, which damaged the premises of several commercial entities. Three foreign nationals – two Belarusians and one Ukrainian, all residing in EU countries – were being investigated in connection with the fire. Romania’s foreign ministry said on Tuesday it had summoned Russia’s ambassador in Bucharest. The Russian embassy in Romania said its ambassador rejected the “baseless” accusations.
France has temporarily relocated a maritime patrol aircraft to ⁠Romania to help identify navigation dangers and bolster the protection of critical energy infrastructure ⁠in the Black ⁠Sea. At least eight cargo ships have been hit ⁠near the coast Romania and Bulgaria in the past three weeks, ⁠with about 34 sailors reported dead or missing. Romania’s defence ministry said on Tuesday the purpose is “to identify dangers to navigation and increase the ability to protect critical infrastructure in Romania’s exclusive ⁠economic zone”.
Poland will host a maintenance centre for the US-made Patriot air-defence system. The centre in Poland will be the only one outside the US, deputy defence minister Sobkowiak-Czarnecka said on social media. Poland, a Nato member bordering Ukraine, serves as a major logistics hub for military aid sent by Kyiv’s allies. Patriot interceptor missiles are regarded as among Ukraine’s most important air-defence assets as it seeks to repel escalating Russian missile and drone attacks.
Pope Leo XIV’s chief almsgiver, Monsignor Luis Marín de San Martín, on Tuesday began a three-day visit to Ukraine and was bringing several trucks worth of winter clothes, blankets and food to Kyiv for distribution. Marín de San Martín was planning to visit the capital, Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro and Fastiv, Vatican News said. Leo had called for a ceasefire and the delivery of food and medicine in Oleshky, and the safe and voluntary evacuation of its people during a phone calls with Putin and Zelenskyy.

Intel’s stock suffered one of its worst days ever on Friday, crashing around 28% after the chip giant reported a weaker-than-expected outlook for the fourth quarter.
This rout reduced the value of Intel’s holdings by the government by $12 billion, CNBC reports . The Trump administration had the government buy 10% stake over a year ago. Nvidia, which also took a big stake in Intel in 2025, saw its stock drop a bit on Friday as well. Much of the tech industry — especially chipmakers — were caught in the sell-off.
Intel’s stock is still a profitable investment for the government so far (and for Nvidia), as it’s up more than 70% for the year, even if it’s dropped significantly from the sky-high prices it commanded over the summer.
The scare-off was caused when Intel warned to expect revenue of $15 billion to $16 billion in the fourth quarter when analysts were looking for around $17 billion. It also warned that its gross profit margin would decline to 37% from 43%, and it was investing so heavily, it expected no positive cash flow.
The main problem for Intel is that PC sales are being hurt by the AI industry gobbling memory and other components, and causing PC prices to rise .
“Our customers began signaling a PC slowdown based on the memory prices and availability. Year-to-date system endpoint prices have increased significantly, placing additional pressure on already limited IT budgets,” Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan warned on the call.
The bright side is that revenue from Intel’s data center business grew 78% over the year-ago quarter. But it is hamstrung on that front until it can bring more capacity to its fabs and book more external customers for them, competing with powerhouse Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co . One of Intel’s new fabs in Arizona is operational but the next one isn’t expected to be online until 2028.

articles.title_zh: China Claims GJ-21 Naval UCAV has Flown from Type 076 Sichuan LHD
articles.content_orig:
China’s GJ-21 naval Unmanned Combat Aerial Vehicle (UCAV) has reportedly conducted its first takeoff and landing aboard the Type 076 Sichuan amphibious assault ship, the Chinese military announced on Oct. 30, 2026 . The development was first reported by state news agencies Xinhua and Global Times , and subsequently publicized by the Ministry of National Defense and the official China Military Bugle social media account.
The military described the GJ-21 as the country’s “first ship-borne stealth reconnaissance and attack drone,” saying that it “recently made its first successful take-off and landing on 076 amphibious assault ship, the ‘Sichuan’.” However, neither the state press nor the military released any official image or video of the actual flight operations.
The development comes as the U.S. Navy advances its own MQ-25 Stingray unmanned aerial refueler program. Primarily designed as a carrier-based tanker, the MQ-25 will also provide a secondary maritime intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) capability. The Stingray is expected to help mature the technologies and operational concepts needed for unmanned carrier aviation, laying the groundwork for the Navy’s future Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) fleet.
The GJ-21 has so far been associated with the Type 076, but future operations from conventional aircraft carriers have also been suggested, with speculation about the drone eventually operating from Fujian, China’s newest carrier. In our previous reports, we have assessed that the GJ-21 could provide an amphibious task group with an embarked unmanned ISR-and-strike capability, potentially extending reconnaissance and precision-attack options beyond the ship’s immediate surroundings
China’s first ship-borne stealth reconnaissance and attack drone “GJ-21” recently made its first successful take-off and landing on 076 amphibious assault ship, the “Sichuan” (Hull 51).
This is another significant breakthrough in the development of China’s amphibious assault ship, indicating that the Chinese Navy now has the capability to operate fixed-wing stealth drones from large maritime combat platforms.
Launched on December 27, 2024, the Sichuan (Hull 51) is the first vessel of Type 076 amphibious assault ships designed and developed independently by China. It incorporates the automatic carrier landing guidance system, new integrated power system, and electromagnetic catapult-assisted takeoff and arrested landing technology, and is capable of carrying fixed-wing unmanned aircraft, helicopters, and amphibious equipment, etc.
Since its first sea trial in November 2025, the Sichuan warship has been steadily conducting various maritime tests as planned, successfully completing the debugging of various equipment and overall operational stability tests.
#AmphibiousAssaultShip #DroneCarrier
#CatapultLaunchSystem #EMALS
#ChinaMilitary #ChinaMilBugle
— China Military Bugle (@ChinaMilBugle) October 30, 2026
The official China Military Bugle account emphasized the PLA Navy’s “capability to operate fixed wing stealth drones from maritime combat platforms.” The statement added:
“[The Sichuan] incorporates the automatic carrier landing guidance system, new integrated power system, and electromagnetic catapult-assisted takeoff and arrested landing technology, and is capable of carrying fixed-wing unmanned aircraft, helicopters, and amphibious equipment, etc. Since its first sea trial in November 2025, the Sichuan warship has been steadily conducting various maritime tests as planned, successfully completing the debugging of various equipment and overall operational stability tests.”
🇨🇳Type 076 + GJ-21 Stealth Drone Swarm🤙
China’s Type 076 amphibious assault ship is being fitted with the GJ-21 stealth carrier-based UAV. Flying-wing design, fluidic thrust vectoring for autonomous carrier landings, electromagnetic catapult launch. Estimated 30 drones per ship, over 2-ton internal payload, ~2,000 km combat radius and 12+ hours endurance.
Extremely low RCS allows deep stealth penetration to clear air defenses, airfields and anti-ship sites before troops even hit the beach. It can also act as loyal wingman with the J-35.
Unlike the US “Lightning Carrier” concept of F-35B on amphibious ships, limited by vertical takeoff payload and range, plus the risk and cost of every manned jet; the Type 076 uses electromagnetic catapults and stealth UAV swarms for higher launch rate, longer reach, better endurance and zero pilot risk.
This upgrades amphibious warfare from bloody beach assaults into non-contact, industrial-scale stealth suppression.
China knows its priority building advanced defense capabilities for the people! Not war!
#Type076 #GJ21 #StealthUAV #ChinaMilitary #PLANA #AmphibiousAssault #ElectromagneticCatapult #LoyalWingman #F35B #AmazingChina #PeopleFirst #NavalPower #DroneSwarm
— GeoPaul626 (@Paull626) August 10, 2026
Global Times additionally quoted Chinese military analyst Song Zongping, who described the GJ-21’s flight operations from the Sichuan as a “global first” and compared it to the U.S. Navy’s X-47B program. “[The] US X-47B carrier-based drone program was designed for aircraft carriers, yet multiple technical constraints led to its cancellation. By contrast, the GJ-21 program has advanced steadily with an efficient development timeline,” Song told GT .
However, the comparison requires some qualification: the X-47B was an experimental demonstrator that successfully completed a series of carrier-aviation milestones before the UCAS-D (Unmanned Combat Air System – Demonstrator) program concluded in 2015. The Navy subsequently redirected its follow-on unmanned-aircraft effort toward the CBARS (Carrier-Based Aerial-Refueling System) aerial-refueling role, which evolved into the MQ-25 Stingray.
Song further added that the GJ-21 may also operate from China’s other EMALS carrier, the Fujian. He argued that this would help “building the technical know-how for China’s third aircraft carrier to host manned-unmanned teaming, expanding the operational modes of carrier strike groups.”
China’s first Type 076 amphibious assault ship, PLANS Sichuan (Hull 51), has completed the deck marking, and its electromagnetic catapult system and arresting gear have been installed in place.

The announcement provides official confirmation of a capability that had been the subject of considerable open-source speculation. Initial indications of an Electromagnetic Launch System (EMALS) aboard the Sichuan Landing Helicopter Dock (LHD) emerged from photographs taken during the ship’s construction and launch.
Official images of the Sichuan’s introduction in the People’s Liberation Army Navy (PLAN) confirmed the catapult’s presence, but it was still not clear at the time whether it was meant for a drone.
Open-source imagery and reporting provided further indications of progress, suggesting the Sichuan’s EMALS was tested with a sled load . Other imagery published between late 2025 and 2026 showed what appeared to be the GJ-21 flying with its arresting hook lowered , as well as a mockup of the tailless flying wing aircraft on the vessel and an image which appeared to show extended landing gear and a catapult launch bar .

Subsequent official imagery confirmed that the Sichuan was fitted with a catapult and arresting system, with images showing the catapult being tested with trial loads . The Oct. 30 announcement now provides China’s first official confirmation that the ship has conducted takeoff and landing operations with the GJ-21.

articles.title_orig: iOS 27.2 adds two FaceTime features, including a personal favorite
articles.title_zh: iOS 27.2 adds two FaceTime features, including a personal favorite
articles.content_orig:
iOS 27.2 adds new features to Messages , Podcasts , Photos , and more—including some easy-to-miss upgrades to FaceTime. Here’s what’s new.
Dual Capture was added to FaceTime in iOS 27 and quickly became one of my favorite features. Rather than having to choose between showing your face or the rear camera view, Dual Capture lets you show both at once.
iOS 27.2 expands Dual Capture to work on all video calls, even with groups. Previously the feature was limited to one-on-one calls.
If you have an iPhone 17 or newer, all you have to do on a video call is hit the ‘Flip’ button, and by default both the front and back camera will be activated.
It’s a huge upgrade to the FaceTime experience, and especially great if, like in my case, you have young kids running around and want to let grandparents see them and you at the same time.
The only drawback: everyone in the call needs to have iOS 27, iPadOS 27, or macOS 27 installed.
iOS 27.2 makes FaceTime more accessible by adding support for third-party sign language interpreters and live captioning.
Inside the three-dot icon, you’ll find a ‘Sign Language’ button that lets you pick an installed VRS (Video Relay Service) app for direct access to an interpreter. The app will appear as a participant tile in the call with a “Waiting for Interpreter” status, then your interpreter’s name will display after they join.
For third-party live captioning, Apple has a step-by-step support document here that outlines the process. You can also optionally stick with the existing built-in Live Captions feature to have your iPhone add automatic captions. It’s available from Settings ⇾ Apps ⇾ FaceTime ⇾ Live Captions.
If you have an iPhone Duo, iOS 27.2 also introduced a new Edge Light feature that works across multiple video calling apps, including FaceTime.
Edge Light works just like on the Mac , adding a ring of light around the iPhone Duo display to better illuminate your face on calls. It’s a built-in alternative to using a physical ring light.
To enable the feature, open Control Center while on a FaceTime call then hit ‘FaceTime Controls’ and tap ‘Edge Light.’ Once enabled, you can adjust settings like the intensity and color temperature.
Have you tried any of iOS 27.2’s new FaceTime features? Let us know in the comments.
